project.title: ECC Challenges
project.html:
ECC Challenges

A public, distributed Pollard rho search on the Certicom ECC challenges. Sign in at ecc-challenges.com, create an API key, and run one Docker container on a CPU or NVIDIA GPU, or the native worker on a Mac (Metal) or a Windows PC. Your worker sends back distinguished points; the server checks them and looks for a collision.

  • Run a worker: Running a worker covers Docker, Compose, Kubernetes, systemd, Podman, Slurm/Apptainer, Modal, macOS and Windows, on GPU (CUDA, Metal) or CPU (x86-64 and arm64).
  • Work on the code: read CONTRIBUTING.md and the open problems. The local stack runs the whole platform on one machine.
  • Live numbers: status page and /v1/status.

How the gateway is built

ecc-challenges.com is the distributed contribution gateway for the 24 published Certicom ECC challenges. Contributors sign in with GitHub, generate a revocable API key, and run a pinned Linux container on a workstation or cloud provider. The generic v2 worker supports prime and binary fields through 359 bits, with CPU, NVIDIA CUDA and Apple Metal backends that share one arithmetic core (worker/generic/ec_core.h), on Linux, macOS and Windows. Existing ECC2K-130 v1 state keeps its original Frobenius walk and 32-byte record format.

Release status, 19 October 2026: all 24 curves are enabled on the public gateway. The final CPU image passed all-curve checks natively on amd64 and arm64; the final combined CPU/CUDA image passed 336 checks on a RunPod RTX 4090. Bounded live CPU checks passed registration, independently checked checkpoint witnesses, same-run restart and closure on every curve. Short runs emitted production points on ECC2-79 and ECCp-79; these checks do not establish larger-curve point rates or fleet capacity. All validation pods were terminated. See the release receipts and earlier correctness controls.

Both public packages are linked to this repository:

Image Hardware
ghcr.io/aburan28/ecc-challenges-worker:latest Linux amd64 CPU or NVIDIA CUDA
ghcr.io/aburan28/ecc-challenges-worker-cpu:latest Linux amd64 and arm64 CPU

Each image supports all 24 curves. The dashboard provides immutable image digests and each challenge's worker command. FPGA acceleration is deferred.

V2 uploads immutable checksum-bound batches directly to versioned S3, verifies every point relation, and conditionally indexes exact points in DynamoDB. PostgreSQL holds identity, quotas, admission cursors and processing metadata. See the all-curve storage design for namespace binding, sizing, collision safety, compaction and archive reconstruction.

flowchart LR
  GPU[Contributor CPU / GPU container] -->|API key, small control JSON| ALB[WAF + HTTPS ALB]
  ALB --> API[Stateless API tasks]
  GPU -->|checksum-bound direct PUT| S3[Versioned immutable S3 archive]
  API -->|namespace and admission receipts| S3
  API -->|identity, quotas, cursor, outbox| PG[(Private PostgreSQL)]
  PG -->|durable delivery and repair| SQS[Audit queue]
  SQS --> Audit[Full v2 point verification]
  S3 -->|pinned raw version| Audit
  Audit --> Index[Conditional DynamoDB point index]
  Index --> Resolver[Coefficient collision + scalar check]
  Resolver -->|immutable result| S3

This diagram describes v2. The separate legacy ECC2K-130 protocol retains its sampled trail replay and PostgreSQL candidate projection. Historical points are imported one way by scripts/historical_import.py (see operations); new generic points have their own curve/walk namespaces.

Contribute

  1. Open https://ecc-challenges.com, sign in with GitHub, and create an API key. The complete key appears once. Save it in ~/.config/ecc-challenges/api-key with mode 0600.
  2. Set GPU_ID to the device index for this container and create a persistent local data directory for it. Give each GPU a distinct directory; never restart a run with a fresh directory while its earlier seed range is active.
  3. Run the command shown on the dashboard. On Linux, install the NVIDIA Container Toolkit so Docker's --gpus all can expose the card. The worker keeps its run identity and checkpoint in the mounted data directory.

For other environments (CPU-only, Kubernetes, systemd, Podman, Slurm) see Running a worker. For an RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell worker in your own Modal account, follow the Modal worker guide. Start with one bounded worker and check its registration, upload, replay, and index status before adding more.

The container pauses GPU collection when the local upload spool reaches its limit and retries with the same run ID. A server 429 or 503 is a request to back off, not permission to discard the local file. Revoking the key stops uploads for its runs. A key is not an AWS credential: it grants no bucket listing, archive reads or database access. A signed upload capability permits only its exact bounded object write.

What an accepted upload means

For v2, admission checks key/account limits, UUID ownership, namespace, cursor, record alignment and checksum-bound S3 object metadata. Its ACK means the versioned raw bytes and admission receipt are durable. The audit worker then checks every record's DP predicate, curve equation and R=aG+bQ relation before any DynamoDB insertion. A collision rechecks its source receipts and coefficient witnesses, computes the candidate scalar and checks dG=Q. Verified coefficient relations do not attest reported trail lengths, so the site's work and completion figures are estimates from point counts (docs/campaigns.md), not verified work.

The following describes the separate legacy DP32 protocol:

The API checks framing, run ID, canonical DP32 orbit-key shape, body size, cursor, key status, key rate and quota, and global pending capacity. It stores the exact bytes under a checksum-bound, write-once S3 key. A successful upload acknowledges archival and the committed cursor. It does not assert that each record came from the claimed seed.

The first batch of each run is selected for independent replay. Later batches are selected after sealing with probability 1/128. A passing first replay opens indexing for that run; sampled and unselected states remain distinct. All public points are kept in ecc_public.candidate_points, separate from the existing campaign's authoritative table. A failed later replay suspends the run, revokes its key, disqualifies already indexed candidate points, and quarantines its leads. A collision lead triggers exact replay of both trails and a pinned host solver; a separate golden-model multiplication must also check the reported scalar against the challenge points before a lead is marked verified.

These checks contain abuse and preserve evidence, but sparse random sampling cannot certify every point in a batch. Quotas, queue backpressure, operator monitoring, and exact replay of every collision lead remain essential.

Development

uv sync --extra test
# Needs PostgreSQL 16 binaries on PATH (initdb, pg_ctl), or set TEST_POSTGRES_DSN.
# macOS: PATH=/opt/homebrew/opt/postgresql@16/bin:$PATH
uv run python -m pytest -q
aws cloudformation validate-template --template-body file://infra/foundation.yaml
aws cloudformation validate-template --template-body file://infra/data.yaml
aws cloudformation validate-template --template-body file://infra/service.yaml

The integration suite starts isolated PostgreSQL and mocked S3/SQS. It checks key lifecycle, run assignment, upload idempotency, archival, outbox repair, indexing, failed replay quarantine, and the HTTP worker protocol. The audit image builds and runs the pinned arithmetic test before copying the replay binary; its host solver is separately built from a pinned crypto source commit. Source bundles and hashes are under vendor/.

Deployment and capacity

See operations for image publishing, AWS stacks, Squarespace DNS, GitHub OAuth setup, rollout checks, and queue alarms. See admission and capacity for the threat model, rate limits, and the measurable throughput gate. The capacity script accepts observed rates:

python3 scripts/capacity.py --gpus 1000 --steps-per-gpu-second 1000000000 \
  --steps-per-dp 350000000 --index-rows-per-task-second 20000 \
  --audit-seconds-per-record 600 --new-runs-per-hour 100

The numbers in that command are illustrative input, not campaign measurements. Releasing the site to a large fleet requires measured replay time and a sustained arrival/drain test; this is tracked in the capacity problem record.

Source and campaign boundary

The contributor GPU base is the immutable image ghcr.io/aburan28/ecc2k130-worker@sha256:25299db686c6b73bb59edc1b5f6591d917ada4e5d933172a4eca7274a71e9421. The replay source is aburan28/cryptanalysis commit c8cc56d8c98705c7f84a21aae1e042453e0105e6; the scalar resolver source is aburan28/crypto commit 79006eb85a400474e83f6a76fac0dca6b60a8b5d. The isolated S3 seed registry is the admission authority for public run IDs. The original campaign table remains in its own account and is never written by this service. Until its points are imported and backmatched, collision lookup covers new public candidates only. The paper's quantitative claims are governed by the paper's separate evidence and submission process.

contributing.title: Contributing
contributing.html:
Contributing

There are two ways to help: run a worker, or work on the code.

Run a worker

Sign in at ecc-challenges.com, create an API key and run the docker run command your dashboard shows. Running a worker covers every other setup: CPU-only, Compose, Kubernetes, systemd, Podman, Slurm and Modal. If something looks wrong (rejected uploads, a crash, a number on the status page that doesn't add up), open an issue with the worker log. Never paste your API key.

Work on the code

Layout

Path What it is
src/ecc_challenges/ FastAPI website and worker API (app.py), templates, status page
src/ecc_challenges/multicurve/ v2 protocol for all 24 curves: codec, admission, verification, index
worker/ Contributor client and generic CPU/CUDA/Metal engine (generic/ec_core.h is the shared core; CMakeLists.txt builds it on Linux, macOS and Windows); Dockerfile (GPU), Dockerfile.cpu (CPU, amd64/arm64); tests/ runs on every platform with only pytest
deploy/ Ways to run workers (Compose, Kubernetes, systemd, Podman, Slurm) and the local stack
verifier/ Replay and verification code used by the audit image
sql/ PostgreSQL migrations, applied in order
infra/ CloudFormation stacks
scripts/ Deploy, publish and live-check scripts (need AWS credentials)
pool/ Separate small-curve pool and STARK prototype, with its own CI
problems/ Open problems with the evidence needed to close each one
verification/ Committed receipts from release checks

Set up and run the tests

You need Python 3.12+, uv and PostgreSQL 16.

uv sync --extra test
uv run python -m pytest -q

The suite starts its own PostgreSQL if initdb and pg_ctl are on PATH. initdb refuses to run as root; in that case, point the tests at a running server instead:

TEST_POSTGRES_DSN=postgresql://postgres:postgres@127.0.0.1:5432/postgres \
  uv run python -m pytest -q

Use python -m pytest rather than bare pytest so that scripts/ is importable. S3 and SQS are mocked with moto; no AWS account is needed. The worker tests need no database: python -m pytest worker/tests runs them anywhere (set ECC_TEST_ENGINE to test a prebuilt engine, such as a Metal build). scripts/check_deploy.sh checks everything under deploy/ (needs kubectl, kubeconform, docker compose, systemd-analyze and shellcheck).

To run the whole platform locally (site, verifier, emulated AWS and a CPU worker uploading real points), use the local stack. It is the quickest way to try a change to the gateway or the worker end to end.

Pull requests

  • Keep each PR to one change. Explain what it does and how you checked it.
  • Add or update a test for any behaviour change. CI runs the full suite, cfn-lint on infra/, and builds all four images.
  • Anything that touches verification, collision handling or admission needs a test that shows the bad case being rejected, not just the good case passing.
  • Don't claim a speedup or a result without the measurement or receipt behind it. Put receipts under verification/ or link them from the PR.
  • No secrets, keys or account IDs in commits, issues or PR text.

Good places to start

  • The open problems, especially verifier throughput and sustained ingest capacity.
  • Worker kernel performance for the binary and prime field walks.
  • An independent reimplementation of the point and collision checks. A second verifier written from the spec is the best way to catch bugs in the first.
  • Website and docs fixes. Templates are in src/ecc_challenges/templates/; the CSP allows inline styles only, no scripts or external assets.

Reporting a security problem

If you find a way to forge accepted work, read other contributors' data or get around key revocation, please don't open a public issue. Use GitHub private vulnerability reporting instead.

running-a-worker.title: Running a worker
running-a-worker.html:
Running a worker

A worker is one process that walks one curve and uploads distinguished points. It is the same program everywhere; only the packaging differs. Pick the row that matches what you have:

You have Use Files
A Linux box with an NVIDIA GPU and Docker Docker command on your dashboard
Several workers on one machine Docker Compose deploy/docker/
A Kubernetes cluster (CPU or GPU nodes) Kubernetes deploy/kubernetes/
A server where you'd rather not run containers Native install + systemd deploy/native/, deploy/systemd/
A Mac (Apple silicon or Intel), using its GPU through Metal macOS deploy/native/install.sh, deploy/launchd/
A Windows PC (x64 or ARM64) Windows deploy/native/install.ps1
Docker, but managed by systemd systemd + Docker deploy/systemd/ecc-worker-docker@.service
Rootless Podman Podman Quadlet deploy/podman/
A university or lab cluster with Slurm Apptainer + Slurm deploy/hpc/
No hardware, a cloud GPU account Modal, RunPod, any container host

Which curves are open right now? The live site lists them at /v1/campaigns. The 19 October 2026 release enables protocol 2 for all 24 curves. Existing ECC2K-130 protocol 1 workers can keep resuming their bound checkpoints.

Quickest start

On a Mac or a Linux machine without Docker, one command downloads the source, builds the native worker into ~/.local/ecc-challenges, asks for your API key and offers to start it:

curl -fsSL https://ecc-challenges.com/install.sh | sh

On Windows, in PowerShell (it installs to %LOCALAPPDATA%\ecc-challenges):

irm https://ecc-challenges.com/install.ps1 | iex

Both take ECC_CAMPAIGN (default eccp-131) from the environment, for example curl -fsSL https://ecc-challenges.com/install.sh | ECC_CAMPAIGN=ecc2-131 sh, and print the command to start the worker again. They wrap the deploy/native installers described below; the scripts themselves are src/ecc_challenges/install/. Run the same command to update.

Before you start

  1. Sign in at ecc-challenges.com and create an API key. Save it where only you can read it:

    mkdir -p ~/.config/ecc-challenges
(umask 077; cat > ~/.config/ecc-challenges/api-key)   # paste, then Ctrl-D

  2. Pick a curve from the catalog, for example eccp-131 or ecc2-131.

  3. Know the rules every recipe follows:

    • One state directory per worker, kept forever. The worker stores its run ID and checkpoint there and locks it. Don't share it between workers, and don't wipe it while the run is active, or the work since the last upload is lost.
    • At most 8 active runs per account. Additional keys share this limit. Closing a run releases an active slot; the lifetime run limit still applies.
    • Stop with SIGTERM and give it up to two minutes. The worker finishes the current round, uploads what it has and saves. Every recipe here is set up that way.
    • To retire a worker for good, run it once with ECC_ACTION=close. This closes the run on the server and keeps the data directory as a record.

Images

Image For Architectures
ghcr.io/aburan28/ecc-challenges-worker All 24 curves on CPU or NVIDIA GPUs (Turing through Blackwell); ECC2K-130 protocol 1 resume amd64
ghcr.io/aburan28/ecc-challenges-worker-cpu Smaller CPU-only build of the same generic 24-curve worker amd64, arm64

Both public packages are linked to the ecc-challenges repository. The combined image built from this source includes both the CUDA engine and a parallel CPU engine, so its pinned digest works on an amd64 machine with or without a GPU. The smaller CPU-only image is available for arm64 or hosts that cannot pull the CUDA-sized image. Use the digest shown on your dashboard and pin it for anything long-running so a new release doesn't change the code under a run.

The CPU engine in new combined builds uses every core it is given. One worker per machine is the right shape for CPUs; set OMP_NUM_THREADS to limit new builds. For GPUs, run one worker per card.

Hardware coverage

Every implemented backend handles all 24 pinned Certicom instances, including prime and binary fields through 359 bits. Hardware acceleration depends on the backend and host:

Host Worker
Linux x86-64 CPU Combined image or CPU-only image
Linux arm64 CPU, including Graviton CPU-only image
Linux x86-64 NVIDIA GPU, Turing through Blackwell Combined image with CUDA and a compatible host driver
macOS GPU, Apple silicon or Intel Mac with Metal Native worker; Docker's Linux VM does not expose Metal
Linux AMD or Intel GPU CPU image uses the host CPU; no ROCm, OpenCL or SYCL backend is implemented
FPGA instance CPU image can use its host CPU; FPGA acceleration is not implemented

The all-curve CUDA image requires a CUDA 13-capable host driver (Linux R580 or newer). Its CUDA 13.0 engine includes native code for the supported generations; it uses CUDA minor-version compatibility. The NVIDIA driver requirement check remains enabled.

An FPGA backend needs a board-specific kernel or bitstream and host runtime. Mounting an FPGA into a container does not provide the curve arithmetic. Docker images here target Linux; native Windows and macOS workers use the same arithmetic core. A supported backend does not enable a campaign at the gateway: check the live catalog before starting an uploading worker.

Check a new image on your hardware

New builds include a finite offline check for all 24 curves. It needs no API key, does not register a run or alter a checkpoint, and checks actual lane states and distinguished points against the Python reference, including invalid-input rejections. Each backend runs 168 checks. A GPU check checks both CPU and the requested GPU backend; an unavailable requested backend fails.

# Use the image you built or a release that includes --check.
docker run --rm --network none -e ECC_BACKEND=cpu "$ECC_WORKER_IMAGE" --check
docker run --rm --network none --gpus all -e ECC_BACKEND=cuda "$ECC_WORKER_IMAGE" --check

Set ECC_CHECK_OUT to a new directory in a mounted writable volume to retain inputs, outputs and a receipt binding the results to each engine's SHA-256. Without it, temporary check artifacts are removed. These are bounded correctness checks, not throughput measurements or challenge solutions. CI checks both final images and runs the CPU image natively on amd64 and arm64. The publishing workflow requires the CPU checks and verifies that anonymous users can retrieve the published manifests.

Docker

The dashboard shows the exact GPU command, with your image digest. On an amd64 CPU host, use that same digest without --gpus all and ECC_GPU:

ECC_WORKER_IMAGE='ghcr.io/aburan28/ecc-challenges-worker@sha256:c7b58f784a8d8ea62d1649062387e76558d627c166fef14f185b6dab417a6f2e'
mkdir -p "$PWD/ecc-data-eccp-131"
docker run -d --restart unless-stopped --name ecc-eccp-131 \
  --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" --stop-timeout 120 \
  -e ECC_CAMPAIGN=eccp-131 \
  -v "$HOME/.config/ecc-challenges/api-key:/run/secrets/ecc_api_key:ro" \
  -v "$PWD/ecc-data-eccp-131:/data" \
  "$ECC_WORKER_IMAGE"
docker logs -f ecc-eccp-131

The published digest above supports all 24 curves on CPU and CUDA and includes the OpenMP CPU engine. For the smaller CPU-only image, including ARM64, use ghcr.io/aburan28/ecc-challenges-worker-cpu@sha256:3e64885e81d55cbe67552e664ca46a38cc5f7276e6041d211b03fc8d2b0a30d8. The dashboard shows the current pinned images.

Docker Compose

deploy/docker/compose.yaml runs CPU and GPU workers from one ECC_WORKER_IMAGE digest, with a read-only root filesystem, no capabilities and your own UID, so the key can stay mode 0600.

cd deploy/docker
cp example.env .env                      # set ECC_UID/ECC_GID (id -u / id -g), curve, image
install -m 0600 ~/.config/ecc-challenges/api-key api-key
docker compose --profile cpu up -d       # or --profile gpu
docker compose logs -f

For more GPUs, copy the gpu0 service to gpu1 and change ECC_GPU, device_ids and the data directory.

Kubernetes

Workers run as a StatefulSet, not a Deployment: each replica gets its own persistent volume (data-ecc-worker-cpu-0, -1, …), so a rescheduled pod resumes its own run. A Deployment with a shared volume would break the one-directory-per-worker rule.

printf '%s' "$(cat ~/.config/ecc-challenges/api-key)" > deploy/kubernetes/base/api-key
kubectl apply -k deploy/kubernetes/cpu      # or deploy/kubernetes/gpu
kubectl -n ecc-challenges logs -f statefulset/ecc-worker-cpu

Edit the overlay's patch to change the curve, replicas (8 or fewer per key) or the CPU limit. The CPU engine's thread count follows the pod's CPU limit. The GPU overlay requests nvidia.com/gpu: 1 per pod and needs the NVIDIA device plugin or GPU Operator. Pods run as UID 10001 with a read-only root filesystem, no service-account token and the RuntimeDefault seccomp profile.

Scaling down leaves the higher-numbered volumes in place, so scaling back up resumes those runs. To retire one for good, close its run first (see above).

Native install and systemd

For hosts without containers. Needs Python 3.10+, g++ (or clang++) with OpenMP, and optionally nvcc for a CUDA build.

git clone https://github.com/aburan28/ecc-challenges && cd ecc-challenges
sudo deploy/native/install.sh
sudo install -m 0600 ~/.config/ecc-challenges/api-key /etc/ecc-challenges/api-key
sudoedit /etc/ecc-challenges/gpu0.env        # curve, backend, GPU index
sudo systemctl enable --now ecc-worker@gpu0
journalctl -fu ecc-worker@gpu0

The installer builds the engine on your machine, runs its self-test, puts everything under /opt/ecc-challenges and adds the ecc-worker@.service template. Each instance (gpu0, gpu1, cpu, …) reads /etc/ecc-challenges/<instance>.env and keeps state in /var/lib/ecc-challenges/<instance>. The key stays root-only; systemd passes the service a private copy. Without root, use deploy/native/install.sh --prefix ~/.local/ecc-challenges --no-systemd and run ~/.local/ecc-challenges/bin/ecc-worker yourself.

macOS

Apple silicon and Intel Macs run the native worker. The engine is built with both a CPU backend and a Metal backend, and ECC_BACKEND=auto picks Metal when the engine sees a Metal device. Needs the Xcode command line tools (xcode-select --install) and Python 3.10+ (python.org or Homebrew; the /usr/bin/python3 that ships with macOS can be older).

git clone https://github.com/aburan28/ecc-challenges && cd ecc-challenges
deploy/native/install.sh --prefix "$HOME/.local/ecc-challenges"
ECC_CAMPAIGN=eccp-131 ECC_STATE_DIR="$HOME/ecc-data/eccp-131" \
  ECC_API_KEY_FILE="$HOME/.config/ecc-challenges/api-key" \
  "$HOME/.local/ecc-challenges/bin/ecc-worker"

The installer prints the engine's --probe report, which lists the Metal devices it found. It also writes a launchd agent to ~/.local/ecc-challenges/com.ecc-challenges.worker.plist; edit the curve and state directory, copy it to ~/Library/LaunchAgents/ and load it with launchctl bootstrap gui/$(id -u) ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.ecc-challenges.worker.plist. launchctl bootout sends SIGTERM and allows 150 seconds for the worker to save. On a Mac with several GPUs, ECC_GPU is an index into the probe's metal_devices list. The Metal kernel is compiled from the same source as the CPU and CUDA engines and must match the CPU backend bit for bit on all 24 curves before it is trusted (see the checks below). Prefer cmake -S worker -B build if you want a universal (arm64;x86_64) engine or Homebrew's OpenMP.

Windows

Windows 10/11 on x64 or ARM64 runs the native worker with the CPU backend, and with CUDA when the CUDA toolkit is installed (x64). Needs Python 3.10+ from python.org, and Visual Studio 2022 or its Build Tools with the "Desktop development with C++" workload (which includes CMake). In PowerShell:

git clone https://github.com/aburan28/ecc-challenges; cd ecc-challenges
powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File deploy\native\install.ps1
mkdir $env:USERPROFILE\.config\ecc-challenges
notepad $env:USERPROFILE\.config\ecc-challenges\api-key    # paste the key, save
icacls $env:USERPROFILE\.config\ecc-challenges\api-key /inheritance:r /grant:r "${env:USERNAME}:R"
$env:ECC_CAMPAIGN = 'eccp-131'
$env:ECC_STATE_DIR = "$env:USERPROFILE\ecc-data\eccp-131"
& "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\ecc-challenges\bin\ecc-worker.cmd"

Stop it with Ctrl-C; the worker finishes the round, uploads and saves (cmd may then ask "Terminate batch job?"; either answer is fine). The wrapper defaults ECC_API_KEY_FILE to %USERPROFILE%\.config\ecc-challenges\api-key. Each round's checkpoint is written atomically, so a hard stop (closing the window, Task Manager, a reboot) loses at most the round in progress.

systemd with Docker

deploy/systemd/ecc-worker-docker@.service wraps docker run in a unit, with the same /etc/ecc-challenges/<instance>.env files plus ECC_IMAGE and, for a GPU, ECC_DOCKER_ARGS=--gpus all. The container runs as UID 10001, so make the key readable by that group: install -m 0640 -g 10001 key /etc/ecc-challenges/api-key.

Podman

deploy/podman/ecc-worker.container is a Quadlet unit for rootless Podman. The key is a Podman secret, delivered as an environment variable that the worker removes before starting the engine.

podman secret create ecc-api-key ~/.config/ecc-challenges/api-key
mkdir -p ~/.config/containers/systemd
cp deploy/podman/ecc-worker.container ~/.config/containers/systemd/
systemctl --user daemon-reload && systemctl --user start ecc-worker
loginctl enable-linger "$USER"

Apptainer and Slurm

Most HPC clusters run Apptainer (formerly Singularity) instead of Docker. deploy/hpc/ecc-worker.sbatch runs one worker per Slurm array task:

apptainer pull ecc-worker.sif docker://ghcr.io/aburan28/ecc-challenges-worker@sha256:<digest>
ECC_CAMPAIGN=eccp-131 sbatch --array=0-3 deploy/hpc/ecc-worker.sbatch

Slurm sends SIGTERM two minutes before the time limit, so the worker saves before the job ends. Each array index keeps its own state directory under ~/ecc-data, so resubmitting the same array resumes the same runs. Check your cluster's policy on long-running jobs and outbound HTTPS before you start.

Settings

Variable Default Meaning
ECC_CAMPAIGN ecc2k-130 Curve ID from the catalog
ECC_BACKEND auto (CPU-only image: cpu) cuda, metal, cpu, or auto (Metal on a Mac whose engine sees a Metal device, CUDA when nvidia-smi sees a GPU, else CPU)
ECC_GPU unset GPU index for this worker (CUDA device, or Metal device from generic-engine --probe)
OMP_NUM_THREADS all available cores CPU engine threads (also honored by builds without OpenMP)
ECC_LANES GPU (CUDA, Metal) 64, CPU 4 × threads Parallel walks. Fixed for a run once it starts
ECC_STATE_DIR /data Persistent state directory
ECC_API_KEY_FILE /run/secrets/ecc_api_key Key file
ECC_API_KEY unset Key as an environment variable instead of a file
ECC_PROTOCOL 2 for new state 1 only for the original ECC2K-130 GPU walk
ECC_ACTION work close retires the run in this state directory
ECC_API_URL https://ecc-challenges.com Gateway

How each recipe was checked

Every recipe except Apptainer/Slurm was run against the local stack, with uploads verified and indexed by the server:

Recipe Check
CPU image Built for amd64; engine self-test; arm64 engine cross-built and matched amd64 output on five curves under QEMU
Docker Compose docker compose config; CPU service uploaded ecc2k-95 points with read-only rootfs and dropped capabilities
Kubernetes Both overlays render and pass kubeconform -strict for Kubernetes 1.34; the pod's security settings were reproduced under Docker, including stop and resume of the same run
Native install install.sh in a clean Debian container; worker uploaded eccp-89 and eccp-97 points; SIGTERM and SIGINT stop cleanly and resume
systemd units systemd-analyze verify
Podman Quadlet Quadlet generator output checked; the same podman run uploaded eccp-109 points
Apptainer + Slurm Not run: no Slurm cluster available. Reviewed only
GPU paths Not run here (no GPU). The GPU image itself has its own L4 release checks in verification/
macOS (arm64, x86_64) CI Worker platforms: install.sh and CMake builds with Metal, self-test, all-24-curve CPU walk against a Python reference, Metal-vs-CPU parity on all 24 curves where the runner exposes a Metal device, universal binary, plutil -lint on the launchd agent, installed wrapper start-up
Windows (x64, ARM64) CI Worker platforms: install.ps1 under Windows PowerShell 5.1, self-test, all-24-curve CPU walk against a Python reference, file lock and atomic checkpoint, installed wrapper start-up
Linux arm64 native CI Worker platforms: as Windows, plus CMake and install.sh builds
Metal kernel source Type-checked on every CI host with clang's C++ for OpenCL, which enforces address spaces as Metal does; compiled with xcrun metal where the Metal toolchain is installed

modal-workers.title: Modal workers for all Certicom curves
modal-workers.html:
Modal workers for all Certicom curves

The launcher reads the current pinned worker image and enabled campaigns from https://ecc-challenges.com/v1/campaigns. It refuses a disabled campaign or v2 release. It supports all 24 campaign IDs when v2 is enabled. A real L4 passed the all-curve arithmetic controls; final image and contributor canaries are separate release checks.

Install Modal and authenticate with modal token new. Sign in on the website, create a key and save it as a local file readable only by you:

chmod 600 /path/to/ecc_api_key
python3 scripts/modal_worker.py start --key-file /path/to/ecc_api_key \
  --campaign eccp-131 --gpu L4 --workers 1 --hours 1
python3 scripts/modal_worker.py status --campaign eccp-131 --workers 1
python3 scripts/modal_worker.py stop --campaign eccp-131 --workers 1

Replace the campaign with any enabled ID in the catalog. CPU workers use --gpu none --backend cpu. CUDA requires a compatible NVIDIA driver and a supported GPU; the generic binary includes Turing through Blackwell targets. The preserved ECC2K-130 sigma binary is an explicit --protocol 1 path for its original compatible GPU configuration. New workers use protocol 2 by default.

Each (campaign,protocol,worker index) has its own named sandbox and volume. The launcher keeps its state in /data/ecc-state, owned by UID/GID10001 with private directories and mode0600 files. Modal starts the bootstrap as root; the bootstrap resolves Modal's provider-created mount symlink, prepares the child directory, then drops privileges before running the contributor. The API key is kept in an ephemeral mode0600 file outside the persistent volume.

Volumes created by the older launcher are upgraded in place. Registration nonces, checkpoints and pending DP data move into the private child directory before the contributor starts. An atomic migration marker allows a bootstrap interrupted between file moves to continue. If both layouts already contain worker state, startup stops and preserves both copies for operator recovery. Do not remove either checkpoint or create another run to bypass that error.

Keep that identity to resume, and never mount one worker volume into simultaneous workers. Modal volumes commit asynchronously and do not provide distributed file locking. The worker pins round geometry, preserves the DP outbox with advanced states atomically, and can replay already admitted batches using stable batch acknowledgements after an older checkpoint is restored. Losing the checkpoint completely still requires operator recovery; server DP archives remain intact.

The launcher sends the key as a Modal Secret and writes a mode 0600 file inside the sandbox. Keys and signed upload URLs are not logged. Revoke a key on the website when access should stop. GPU time and persistent storage are billed to the contributor's provider account. stop preserves its volume and server data. Start with one worker and inspect upload and backlog status before increasing worker count. The account cap is eight active runs across both protocols.

The bounded, key-free python3 scripts/check_modal_volume.py --out receipt.json check verifies migration, mode0600 ownership, atomic checkpoint writes, two fresh CPU sandboxes and external committed-volume hashes using the exact bootstrap. Its counter data is a filesystem control. A real GPU contribution is a separate release check. Modal documents its Docker USER behavior and volume commit/locking behavior.

RunPod and other Linux container hosts use the same digest shown on the website, a persistent /data volume, and these runtime settings:

Setting Value
ECC_API_URL https://ecc-challenges.com
ECC_CAMPAIGN Any enabled catalog ID, for example ecc2-131
ECC_PROTOCOL 2 for a new generic worker
ECC_BACKEND auto, cuda, or cpu
ECC_API_KEY_FILE Mounted secret path, default /run/secrets/ecc_api_key
ECC_API_KEY Provider environment secret instead of a mounted file
ECC_STATE_DIR /data, backed by a distinct persistent volume per worker

Use either key mechanism. For CPU containers, omit Docker's --gpus option. The worker consumes and removes the environment key before starting native code. Native arithmetic failures preserve the previous durable checkpoint and report an error; they do not silently change the requested CUDA computation.

local-stack.title: Local stack
local-stack.html:
Local stack

deploy/local/compose.yaml runs the whole platform on one machine: the website and worker API, the verification and repair workers, PostgreSQL, emulated S3/SQS/DynamoDB (LocalStack), and optionally a CPU worker. Use it to work on the gateway, the verifier or the worker without an AWS account.

docker compose -f deploy/local/compose.yaml up -d --build
docker compose -f deploy/local/compose.yaml run --rm -T init \
  python scripts/local_stack.py key me > .local-key
chmod 644 .local-key          # the worker container runs as UID 10001
docker compose -f deploy/local/compose.yaml --profile worker up -d --build worker
docker compose -f deploy/local/compose.yaml logs -f worker audit

Open https://localhost:8443 and accept the local certificate. The status page shows points arriving, then verified. A CPU worker finds a point every few seconds on the small curves. To switch curves, stop the worker, remove its state (docker volume rm ecc-local_worker-data), and start it again with ECC_CAMPAIGN=ecc2-131 (or any catalog ID) set in your shell.

Stop with down; add -v to wipe the database, archive and worker state.

How it fits together

Service Role
proxy Caddy with its own local CA. Serves the site as ecc-challenges.test and localhost:8443, and S3 as s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com
localstack S3, SQS and DynamoDB
postgres Accounts, keys, runs, batches
init Applies sql/ (every start; migrations are idempotent), creates the bucket, queues and point table, publishes the CA certificate
web Website and worker API, with all 24 curves enabled
audit Verifies every uploaded point and queues it for the point index
reconcile Delivers queued work, repairs anything left half-done and merges the point index every 30 seconds
worker The CPU worker image, pointed at the local gateway

The worker only talks to an HTTPS gateway and only uploads to *.amazonaws.com, the same checks it makes in production. The stack meets them with the TLS proxy and network aliases rather than by relaxing the worker. Those names exist only on the stack's Docker network.

LocalStack is used instead of moto because the gateway checks two things moto doesn't provide: the SHA-256 checksum S3 records for a signed upload, and DynamoDB's TableId.

The stack uses the compact point index (POINT_INDEX_MODE=compact, see docs/multicurve-storage.md); set POINT_INDEX_MODE=dynamodb in your shell before up to use the DynamoDB index instead. To check collision handling end to end, let a worker upload a few points, then inject a known-answer collision:

docker compose -f deploy/local/compose.yaml run --rm -T \
  -v "$PWD/.local-key:/app/.local-key:ro" init \
  python scripts/local_collision_check.py eccp-79 /app/.local-key

It registers a second run, uploads one of the worker's points written with that run's own coefficients, and passes once the resolver recovers the curve's published reference scalar.

GitHub sign-in isn't configured locally, so the dashboard isn't usable; scripts/local_stack.py key creates keys instead. It refuses to run unless LOCAL_STACK=1, which only this compose file sets.

campaigns.title: Certicom campaigns and public status
campaigns.html:
Certicom campaigns and public status

The Certicom ECC Challenge document, updated November 2009 is the source for the 24 names, field sizes, solution snapshot and historical elliptic-curve-operation estimates in src/ecc_challenges/catalog.py. Section 4 names the challenges, section 6.1 lists the ten solutions then known, and section 6.2 gives the operation estimates. Section 6.2 mislabels the ECC2K-95 and ECC2-97 solved rows as ECC2-79; their solution dates in section 6.1 identify those rows. The website labels all of these as historical. It does not assert that a challenge remains unsolved today.

The public status page and GET /v1/status are served by this application. The database query reads the bounded run table and 16 pressure shards, and is cached for 60 seconds per web task. Runs, queue depth and total_archived_points cover this isolated public gateway only. Points imported from the earlier account (338,034,791 distinct DP32 points on 2026-10-17) are reported beside them as total_historical_points and the ECC2K-130 row's historical_points, read from the ecc_public.historical_import_totals view; the page adds them to the point totals and says so. Every new public point is matched against them. If the web role can't read the view, those fields are null and the page falls back to gateway-only counts.

An uploaded point count is not a count of independently verified operations, so work is reported as an estimate (src/ecc_challenges/work.py). Each stored point stands for the mean walk length between distinguished points: 2^28.41 steps on the ECC2K-130 sigma walk, where DP32 means normal-basis Hamming weight <= 32 among the 2^130 even-weight x (not 32 zero bits), and 2^d for a v2 namespace pinned to d DP bits. Each walk on a curve (the sigma walk, and each pinned v2 namespace) is counted separately. Each open row carries:

  • estimated_operations_2009_log2: Certicom's estimate as a power of two.
  • estimated_work_operations and estimated_work_log2: estimated steps behind the stored points.
  • expected_operations_log2: expected steps for the campaign's default walk, sqrt(pin/(4131)) for the sigma walk and sqrt(pi*n/2) for the v2 walk, which has no automorphism quotient yet.
  • expected_work_percent and estimated_completion_probability_percent: work as a share of that expectation, and 1 - exp(-(pi/4)*(k/E)^2), the chance rho would have produced a collision by now. Separate walks on one curve add their (k/E)^2 terms.
  • points_per_hour, operations_per_second_log2 and hours_to_expected_work, over a 24-hour window.

These top-level figures count this gateway's public runs; ECC2K-130's including_historical repeats them with the imported points added to the sigma walk. The snapshot adds total_estimated_work_log2 and total_estimated_work_log2_including_historical. The estimates assume honest walks and a random-looking walk, and lag the steps still inside unfinished trails. A frozen work counter with independently checked checkpoints remains the way to turn them into verified figures. A Pollard rho search has no deterministic fraction complete; /pollard-rho explains the model on the site.

Contribution compatibility

The current public image runs the ECC2K-130 Frobenius walk. Its state directory is bound to ecc2k-130; the worker sends that campaign identity to the gateway and refuses another selection. The gateway rejects registration for other campaigns and returns HTTP 409 for their configuration requests. The catalog still lists them so the site can represent the complete published set without admitting unverifiable data.

The same image and API key can be run with Docker on a local GPU, a RunPod container, or any host with an NVIDIA runtime, persistent /data, and outbound HTTPS. The Modal guide uses a Modal Secret and Volume to provide those same two things. Each container needs a distinct persistent state directory. The image is pinned by digest on the dashboard. For a RunPod Pod, select that image, attach a persistent or network volume at /data, set ECC_STATE_DIR=/data and ECC_CAMPAIGN=ecc2k-130, and inject the website key as ECC_API_KEY. The worker removes that variable before launching the CUDA process. Provider settings that contain the key remain sensitive; a read-only mounted file at /run/secrets/ecc_api_key is preferred where available.

Adding a new campaign requires, in order:

  1. Import and independently check Certicom's exact field, curve, subgroup and target points; pin the parameter transcript and a known-answer test.
  2. Implement the worker walk, record format, checkpoint, and independent replay for that campaign. A name in the catalog is not an executable worker.
  3. Give the campaign its own run namespace, archive prefix, point index, collision queue, rate and storage budgets. Include the campaign and walk version in every signed or hashed identity and every database uniqueness key. No ECC2K-130 seed or orbit key can be reused across curves.
  4. Exercise one contributor end to end: key issue, registration, upload, archival, replay, indexing, collision lead and independent scalar check. Run sustained arrival and drain measurements before opening a large fleet.
  5. Mark the catalog entry's contribution ready only after those checks pass.

The existing pool/ prototype offers a prime-field reference walk and audit ideas. Its SQLite server and generated sample curves are not a Certicom production backend. The current SQL schema, DP32 binary record, CUDA image, replay binary and scalar resolver are specific to ECC2K-130 and must be generalized or separately deployed for other curves. The concrete exit gate is tracked in the multi-campaign problem record.

V2 implementation

The generic all 24 path now lives under src/ecc_challenges/multicurve/ and worker/generic/. See storage and validation and provider commands. The exact registry supersedes field widths in the summary table when they disagree: notably Appendix A's ECCp-191 modulus has 191 bits. All v2 namespaces bind that exact instance, target and walk. The v1 routes remain specific to the original ECC2K-130 Frobenius encoding. A new empty volume selects v2; an existing state.json resumes v1 unless the operator explicitly selects another protocol. A directory from one campaign or protocol is never silently reassigned.

admission-and-capacity.title: Admission, abuse limits, and drain capacity
admission-and-capacity.html:
Admission, abuse limits, and drain capacity

Protocol scope

This service has two isolated protocols. The sections below describe the legacy ECC2K-130 DP32 path. The generic v2 path supports all 24 published Certicom instances using 56–196-byte affine coefficient records; see v2 storage and recovery.

V2 uses tiny authenticated JSON control messages at https://ecc-challenges.com/v2/. Checksum/length/type/encryption-bound S3 PUT capabilities carry the raw bytes directly, so large uploads do not occupy web tasks. Every record must satisfy the namespace's DP predicate, curve equation and R=aG+bQ relation before any DynamoDB index write. UUID runs and hashed curve/target/walk/codec namespaces isolate the campaigns. Claimed step counts are not credited as verified work.

V2 admission limits include eight outstanding reservations and 32 pending batches per account, eight active runs across both protocols, the shared daily byte quota, and a sharded global cap initially 512 pending v2 batches. Rejected new intents receive 429 (account) or 503 (global shard) with Retry-After; they do not obtain an upload capability. Admitted batches remain recoverable from immutable S3 objects, PostgreSQL state and receipts even if SQS delivery or a worker fails. The reconciler repairs stale unfinished work. Completed runs can be explicitly closed without recycling identity or discarding admitted data.

The audit service performs v2 verification, conditional DynamoDB indexing and collision resolution. Increasing the legacy index or resolver pools adds no v2 drain capacity. V2 capacity planning must measure complete verification and indexing per curve/record width, source-object and receipt requests, PostgreSQL coordination, DynamoDB writes and duplicates, queue age, autoscaling, and total cost. scripts/capacity.py only models legacy sampled replay and must not be used to estimate v2 capacity.

The live all 24 single-point canaries establish contribution correctness. A bounded duplicate-record backlog/recovery check establishes only its stated admission and restart behavior. Neither defines a sustained fresh-point rate or a global GPU fleet size. The configured 32-auditor maximum also depends on the account's effective Fargate vCPU quota; it is 30 before the pending 256 request. Public opening must name the measured operating envelope and retain admission caps rather than treating autoscaling as unlimited capacity.

Legacy protocol

The public endpoint is https://ecc-challenges.com/v1/ on an AWS Application Load Balancer in us-west-2, behind AWS WAF and two Global Accelerator static addresses. Squarespace remains the DNS provider. ECS web tasks are stateless; the dedicated private rho_dp PostgreSQL instance stores cursors and indexed public candidates, while the new account's S3 bucket holds raw batches.

Trust boundaries

Input or asset Boundary and control Meaning after control
GitHub identity OAuth callback, secure signed session, CSRF on key forms Contributor can manage only their account's keys
API key 256-bit secret shown once, HMAC digest with Secrets Manager pepper, constant-time comparison, revocation Authenticated upload principal; no cloud credential
Run ID Isolated S3 seed registry uses conditional create Seed namespace is reserved before assignment
DP upload 1 MiB body maximum, structural checks, cursor lock, immutable checksum S3 write Bytes are durably archived, not mathematically validated
Replay Post-seal random selection; first batch mandatory; exact pinned host walk Sampled record either matches, fails, or stays unverified
Collision Both trails replayed, pinned host scalar solver, separate golden-model scalar multiplication, result receipt in S3 A verified scalar requires both independent point checks

The WAF blocks more than 10,000 requests per 5 minutes from one IP, and more than 300 per 5 minutes for authentication or key routes. Both rate rules return HTTP 429 with Retry-After 60, so shared-provider throttling is retryable rather than a permanent permission error. The application has a 240-token per-key burst bucket refilling 4 tokens/s; a 1 MiB DP upload costs 16 tokens. A key is limited to 5 GiB/day across DP batches and checkpoints, and an account to three active keys, eight active runs, and 64 lifetime run IDs. The pending batch counter is sharded 16 ways and admission returns 503 with Retry-After when the configured backlog bound is hit. The contributor sends a remote checkpoint at most every 15 minutes by default and pauses its GPU when the local spool fills rather than discarding unsent records.

These limits make abuse bounded per key and IP, but they do not prevent an attacker from acquiring many GitHub accounts or using many networks. WAF and per-key quotas are cost controls; the independent replay and candidate quarantine protect result integrity. A determined attacker can still consume storage and verifier capacity. Operators must watch WAF blocks, account enrollment, S3 growth, queue age, and daily AWS spend, and lower quotas or temporarily close admission if those diverge from the measured plan.

The current public run allocation is 50000..65534, or 15,535 unique run IDs over the lifetime of this campaign. IDs are never recycled because the seed is (run_id << 48) | local_counter. The lifetime account cap limits one account's ability to consume that finite namespace; operators can adjust it after reviewing contributor needs and remaining IDs. A larger contributor population needs a registry audit for additional unused IDs or a new campaign/seed format; autoscaling HTTP tasks cannot expand this namespace.

Queue and database design

The ingest ACK follows an S3 conditional PutObject plus one PostgreSQL transaction for the cursor, quota, pressure count, and outbox row. A retry at the same byte offset and digest is idempotent; a different digest gets 409. An outbox reconciler repairs a lost SQS send after the database commit. SQS delivery may repeat, so audit, index, and resolve workers use durable status rows and unique constraints. Audit, index, and collision each have their own queue and dead-letter queue. Audit and indexing scale independently, avoiding large DP joins on the HTTP request path.

Admission checks whether a pressure shard is full before the S3 write, then atomically increments its count after the bounded write. The shard row is not locked across S3 network I/O, so unrelated runs can upload concurrently. If another upload fills it between those checks, the request returns 503; its write-once object can be reused by an exact retry after capacity clears.

The candidate index has 32 hash partitions on the 24-byte orbit key. Each index task bulk copies one sealed batch into a temporary table, joins that batch to the new account's public.distinguished_points projection through its (campaign_id,point_key) key, and inserts public candidates idempotently. That historical projection starts empty until the later verified import and backmatch; current collision lookup covers new public points against each other. The historical table is read-only to the worker role. A failed later audit marks its run's prior candidates disqualified and its leads quarantined. Source objects and audit receipts stay immutable for review.

Capacity gate

Let G be active GPUs, s measured walk steps/GPU/s, L measured mean steps per DP, B records/batch, q measured index rows/task/s, T measured seconds to replay one selected record, and R new runs/hour. Approximate rates are:

DP arrival/s       = G·s/L
batch arrival/s    = G·s/(L·B)
audit selections/s = R/3600 + max(0, batch arrival/s - R/3600)/128
index task need    = ceil(headroom · DP arrival/s / q)
audit task need    = ceil(headroom · audit selections/s · T)

Use scripts/capacity.py with measured values and at least 2× headroom. Autoscaling targets are capped at eight index tasks and 32 audit tasks. Those caps protect the private RDS instance and cost; exceeding them requires a deliberate measured change, not a larger queue. The service returns backpressure before the pending bound is exceeded. A queue that grows continuously at the projected peak is an admission failure even if HTTP uploads still return 201.

Before a global opening, run a sustained, production-shaped load on the release images with distinct valid run IDs and sealed DP32 objects. Record arrival and drain rates over the same interval, p50/p95 replay seconds, index rows/s, S3 request error rate, RDS CPU/IOPS/locks/connections, ECS scale events, queue visible/in-flight/oldest age, dead-letter counts, end to end bytes, and actual cloud cost. Repeat after a task restart and an injected SQS send failure. Require the queues to return to baseline after traffic stops and every acknowledged object to be indexed or explicitly retained as unverified/quarantined. Compare the measured peak to the intended GPU fleet; record the largest fleet that passed. The current DP32 replay throughput and this sustained gate are tracked in the linked problem record.

Database network boundary

The public service uses a private RDS instance in its dedicated AWS account and VPC. PostgreSQL ingress is limited to that VPC's CIDR, and both service roles use verified TLS and limited SQL privileges. The original campaign's rho-dp security group is outside this platform and remains a separate legacy exposure; it should be narrowed through a coordinated inventory of its existing ingesters. The public service has no network route or credential to that owner database.

multicurve-storage.title: All-curve distinguished-point storage
multicurve-storage.html:
All-curve distinguished-point storage

Implementation status: v2 is being integrated and is disabled by default. The production ECC2K-130 v1 walk keeps its existing encoding and namespace. A catalog entry alone never enables a worker. The ECC2K-130 v1 historical import is separate; see operations.md.

Scope and identities

Support covers the 24 instances in Appendix A of the official Certicom challenge document: 9 prime-field and 15 binary-field instances, with actual field widths 79–359 bits. src/ecc_challenges/multicurve/instances.json pins the PDF, extracted text, exact polynomial basis, coefficients, G, Q, subgroup order and cofactor. Recorded source normalizations are reproducible with extract_parameters.py. Probable-prime checks are arithmetic admission checks, not primality certificates.

A namespace SHA-256 binds the exact instance digest, target Q, walk, DP predicate, coefficient derivation and record codec. UUID runs and 64-bit trail IDs remove the legacy 16-bit run allocation constraint. No record crosses namespaces, including records for the same curve using different walks. The generic affine walk uses 32 deterministic nonzero G multiples; start coefficients use full-width SHAKE256 rejection sampling. Binary arithmetic uses the published polynomial basis.

Each record stores trail_id:u64le | steps:u64le | x:BE | y:BE | a:BE | b:BE, where R=aG+bQ. Widths are fixed per namespace, derived from field and subgroup sizes: 56–196 bytes for this registry. Scalars are binary, avoiding database numeric precision limits. Finite points whose SHA-256 of canonical x||y has trailing DP bits zero qualify; the first hash byte selects the walk partition. V1 retains its original DP32 Frobenius predicate.

DP bits are set per curve (dp_bits_for in multicurve/codec.py). This walk has no automorphism quotient, so a solve takes about E = sqrt(pi*n/2) steps. The rule is d = floor(log2 E) - 23, capped at 34. With up to 2^16 walks running at once, the steps left in unfinished walks stay under 1% of E, and each curve below the cap needs about 2^23.5 (~12 million) DPs. ECCp-79 gets 16 bits, ECCp-109 31, and every curve of 130 bits or more 34 (ECC2K-130 about 2^30.8 DPs, ECCp-131 about 2^31.4). The DP bit count is part of the namespace, so changing the rule starts new namespaces; existing runs keep the setting pinned in their manifest.

Every trail keeps the b of its start, because jumps add only multiples of G. Verification therefore also checks that each DP's b equals the start derived from its run ID and trail ID, which ties the DP to a server-assigned trail without replaying the walk. It does not check the trail's a or step count.

Submission and processing

flowchart LR
    C[Contributor container] -->|API key + intent metadata| A[HTTPS admission API]
    A -->|reserve quota and backlog| P[(PostgreSQL metadata)]
    A -->|short-lived signed PUT| C
    C -->|immutable bytes + checksum| S[(Versioned private S3)]
    C -->|authenticated commit| A
    A -->|HEAD size + checksum + version| S
    A -->|immutable admission receipt| S
    A -->|transactional outbox| P
    P --> Q[SQS verification queue]
    Q --> V[Bounded verification workers]
    V -->|full point relation checks| S
    V -->|conditional exact-point insertion| D[(DynamoDB point index)]
    D --> L[Collision lead + scalar verification]
    L --> S
    S --> X[Sorted compact segments / index rebuild]
  1. An authenticated upload intent reserves a byte quota and a backlog slot before issuing any S3 capability. At most one reserved intent exists at a run cursor, and at most eight exist per account. Intents expire after 15 minutes.
  2. A signed PUT fixes object key, content length, SHA-256 checksum, content type, server-side encryption and If-None-Match: *. Contributors receive no AWS credentials and cannot list, read, delete or choose archive keys.
  3. Commit reauthenticates the API key and run, checks the uploaded length and checksum with HEAD, and pins the S3 VersionId. Immutable batch and admission receipts describe the accepted bytes. Successful acknowledgment requires the admission receipt. A durable database outbox repairs interrupted queue sends.
  4. A verifier checks the raw SHA-256 and namespace binding, canonical coordinates and scalars, DP predicate, curve equation, and every R=aG+bQ relation. Only fully validated batches produce verified receipts and index writes. A lease token guards progress and terminal updates. Retry cannot skip an unfinished record or use another verifier's uncommitted progress.
  5. Each exact point uses a conditional DynamoDB PutItem with attribute_not_exists(pk) and ReturnValuesOnConditionCheckFailure=ALL_OLD. The prior witness is returned on a collision. This avoids a lookup/insert race and preserves the first immutable witness. Identical coefficient pairs are duplicate work; distinct pairs create deterministic collision leads.
  6. A batch is indexed only after all point inserts and collision leads are durable. For equal points, solve (a1-a2)/(b2-b1) mod n, then check dG=Q. A zero denominator is recorded as degenerate. All result receipts remain in S3. A retry after an index insert recreates any interrupted lead.

SQS is at least once: leases, immutable object keys and idempotent records are required. SQS depth is not an authoritative ledger. Reconciliation requeues unfinished database rows, including messages that expired or reached a DLQ.

Archive layout

public-gateway/<stream>/v2/
  namespaces/<namespace>/manifest.json
  raw/<namespace>/shard=<sha256-prefix>/runs/<uuid>/<byte-offset>-<sha256>.bin
  batches/<namespace>/<batch-uuid>/<receipt-sha256>.json
  admissions/<namespace>/<batch-uuid>/<receipt-sha256>.json
  checkpoints/<namespace>/<batch-uuid>/<receipt-sha256>.json
  verified/<namespace>/<batch-uuid>/<receipt-sha256>.json
  collisions/<namespace>/<lead-id>/<receipt-sha256>.json
  compaction/<namespace>/<segment-id>/<receipt-sha256>.json
  segments/<namespace>/<segment-sha256>.bin

Raw objects and receipts use conditional writes and versioning. Service roles have no object deletion permission. Bucket policy enforces conditional writes for v2. S3 remains the witness archive; PostgreSQL holds account/run/cursor, quota, processing and collision metadata. DynamoDB is a rebuildable online index. PostgreSQL account secrets and quota history still require database backups.

Do not create one S3 object per DP. Contributors upload batches up to 1 MiB; compaction groups verified batches into sorted segments targeting 128–256 MiB. A segment retains the source batch UUID and record ordinal for every witness, plus a manifest naming all source checksums and versions. Compaction never removes raw witnesses. Lifecycle rules may move old compact segments to cheaper storage after their minimum storage and access requirements are understood.

Compact point index

POINT_INDEX_MODE=compact replaces the DynamoDB index with sorted 16-byte entries in S3 (multicurve/pointindex.py). Uploads and verification are unchanged: workers still send full records, every record is still checked, and the raw batch stays the authority. Only the index is smaller.

public-gateway/<stream>/pointindex/<namespace>/parts/<part>-<sha256>.bin
public-gateway/<stream>/v2/pointindex/<namespace>/generation-<n>/<receipt-sha256>.json
Bytes Field Meaning
0–7 fingerprint first 8 bytes of SHA-256(x‖y), the digest the walk already computes
8–15 locator index_seq (40 bits) ‖ record index (24 bits), big-endian
  1. Indexing a verified batch only gives it the next index_seq (dp_index_seq, in PostgreSQL). Nothing is written per point.
  2. The reconcile task merges every POINT_INDEX_MERGE_SECONDS (or run python -m ecc_challenges.queues merge once). For each namespace with pending batches it reads their raw objects (version- and SHA-256-pinned), makes one entry per distinct (point, witness), and merges them into parts: 4,096 sorted files, one per top 12 fingerprint bits.
  3. Each new fingerprint is looked up in its part. A shared fingerprint is resolved from the full records: the same point with another witness becomes a collision lead and is solved as before; the same witness is duplicate work, whose entry is dropped and counted as deduplicated; a different point is a fingerprint false positive (about N²/2⁶⁵ of them for N entries, so roughly 0.1 for a full ECC2K-130 solve).
  4. A generation manifest (parts, checksums, counts, leads) is written under v2/, then committed by compare-and-swap on dp_point_index, together with the batches it covers and their duplicate counts. Parts the new generation replaced are deleted; a lifecycle rule expires their old versions after 7 days. Parts live outside v2/, which forbids deletes.

The index is derived. Merger.rebuild(namespace) discards it, and the next merges rebuild it from every indexed batch; counters are adjusted by the difference, so a rebuild leaves them unchanged. Batches indexed while the mode was dynamodb have no index_seq and stay in DynamoDB only.

Sizing: a merge rewrites every part that received entries, so its cost grows with the index (16 bytes per entry). ECC2K-130 at DP34 is about 2^30.8 entries, about 30 GB in S3 (under $1 a month) against about 1 TB of DynamoDB items. Merging the part lists is fast (30 million existing plus 1 million new entries in about 4 s of CPU); S3 transfer dominates. Below about 100 million entries hourly merges are cheap. Above that, merge daily (POINT_INDEX_MERGE_SECONDS=86400). A collision is found at the first merge after both points are indexed.

Capacity, abuse and accounting

API tasks scale behind the existing HTTPS load balancer. Direct S3 upload keeps DP bytes off web task memory and network paths. Verification and conditional index insertion scale independently from admission. Limit in-flight work per worker; do not submit an unbounded future per point. Autoscale against oldest queue age and sustained backlog, and monitor verifier rate, index throttle count, failed validation, duplicate rate, DLQs and reserved-byte utilization.

Admission stops issuing capabilities when bounded pressure pools fill and returns Retry-After. Clients retain pending records and checkpoint state, pause compute during failed upload, and retry with backoff. v1 and v2 have separately bounded pressure pools; their sum is the overall maximum. Keys share an account run cap and daily byte accounting; there is no anonymous ingestion route.

Full algebraic verification establishes a valid point relation. It does not prove the submitted path, elapsed GPU work, independence, or claimed step count. An attacker can still send duplicate valid witnesses; deduplication and quotas bound their impact. Do not convert reported steps into verified work. Progress percentages remain unknown until a declared work-verification and collision model exists. Audited walk segments or unpredictable replay challenges are a separate future scoring gate.

For capacity planning, raw bytes/day = 86400 * DP/s * record_bytes before compression and replicas. Conditional index write units/day are approximately 86400 * DP/s * write_attempts_per_DP * ceil(item_bytes/1024); failed conditions and retries also consume capacity. At 10,000 DP/s, raw records alone are 48.384–169.344 decimal GB/day across current widths. This is arithmetic sizing, not a measured ingest rate. Every-curve verification cost, provider GPU controls, and sustained end-to-end capacity must be measured before advertising a rate. Prewarm DynamoDB capacity and request quota increases for the intended launch rate; on-demand mode does not guarantee an unlimited instantaneous burst.

Required launch checks

  • Exact registry validation and all ten published scalar correctness vectors.
  • All 24 native CPU transitions checked against the independent Python group implementation, including wide limbs, identities and malformed encodings.
  • The same finite controls on a real NVIDIA GPU using the published image.
  • Presigned mutation rejection, quota/backlog boundaries, revoked keys and cross-namespace submissions, plus concurrent first-point collision controls.
  • Interrupted upload/commit/verification/indexing and expired-message recovery.
  • Archive-driven index reconstruction and compaction checksum verification.
  • Measured sustained ingest with declared DP/s, item widths, verification rate, queue-age limits, duplicates, retries, cost and headroom.

Sources: DynamoDB PutItem, S3 conditional writes, S3 HEAD checksums and versions, SQS delivery semantics, DynamoDB on-demand scaling.

Operator tools

The exact verified receipt list is an explicit bounded input, in a JSON array. Use a role scoped to the archive and the separate rebuild table. The tool checks its AWS account before any mutation. A rebuild checks every relation again, preserves every collision in S3, and emits completion only after durable leads.

python -m ecc_challenges.multicurve.archive_tool compact \
  --profile ecc-challenges-new --expected-account ACCOUNT_ID \
  --bucket ecc-challenges-data-ACCOUNT_ID --campaign eccp-131 \
  --verified-keys /path/to/verified-keys.json --max-input-mib 128
python -m ecc_challenges.multicurve.archive_tool rebuild \
  --profile ecc-challenges-new --expected-account ACCOUNT_ID \
  --bucket ecc-challenges-data-ACCOUNT_ID --campaign eccp-131 \
  --verified-keys /path/to/verified-keys.json \
  --target-table ecc-challenges-rebuild-20261016 --max-input-mib 128

Provision the destination rebuild table with the same pk string schema. The operator must compare complete source coverage and collision receipts before switching a service to the rebuilt table. Account/run metadata comes from PostgreSQL backups; the index tool does not restore OAuth or quota history. For archives beyond one256MiB group, run disjoint explicit receipt groups against the same destination with --resume; retain every group's completion receipt.

Verification workers bind the DynamoDB creation UUID (TableId) to a durable PostgreSQL row on their first startup, before any batch has been indexed. A table recreated under the same name fails this fence. Worker roles can insert and read the binding but cannot update or delete it. Rebuilds target a separate name; only an operator can activate a complete rebuilt generation after checking all completion and collision receipts. Stop workers during that operation.
