operations.html:
Operations and release sequence

The public platform belongs in its own AWS account in us-west-2. Squarespace manages DNS for ecc-challenges.com. The original ECC2K campaign remains in account ACCOUNT_ID; do not connect the public service to its RDS instance or S3 bucket. The deployment scripts require a named AWS profile and the expected 12-digit account ID, then verify the active AWS identity before writing. Configure credentials locally and rotate any credential that was exposed. Never put a secret value in chat, a shell command, a PR, or a tracked file.

What the new account owns

  • The foundation stack: private ECR repositories, three durable queues with dead-letter queues, and generated application secrets.
  • The data stack: a dedicated VPC, a private encrypted Multi-AZ PostgreSQL instance, a versioned private S3 archive, an empty historical-point table, a GitHub App sign-in secret placeholder, and a one-off ECS administration task.
  • The service stack: HTTPS ALB, WAF rate rules, stateless web and queue workers, separate autoscaling, queue alarms, and Global Accelerator.

The historical-point table starts empty. New public uploads are archived, audited, indexed, and matched against other new public points. Matches with the original campaign's existing points are unavailable until the historical import and backmatch below have run. This is not a reason to leave the new index queue stopped: every new batch and candidate is preserved, and the backmatch covers the interval before import.

The old campaign's run registry currently has no entries in the public range 50000–65534 (read-only check on 2026-10-14). Reserve that range for the public service in both accounts. The isolated registry uses the same format but has its own S3 bucket; do not let the original allocator use public run IDs.

Historical point import

scripts/historical_import.py copies the original campaign's points into public.distinguished_points in one direction. It never connects the public service to the original account: the operator runs the export with a read-only profile for account ACCOUNT_ID, and the public database never sees that account's credentials. The original S3 dp/ corpus is the source, because the original RDS table is a derived view that can lag it.

  1. export --dry-run lists and checks the whole corpus and writes nothing. It refuses any object whose .bin.json marker or key sha256 disagrees with its body, and drops (and counts) records that are not canonical DP32 keys or whose seed falls in the public run range 50000–65534. Read its summary before going on.
  2. export --parts s3://<public archive>/historical-import/<date> writes each source object as a checksum-bound part with a JSON sidecar. It resumes by skipping source keys that already have a sidecar.
  3. load runs with the database owner's DSN in HISTORICAL_DSN. Each part is re-hashed, inserted with ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING, and recorded in ecc_public.historical_import_parts in the same transaction, so a rerun skips finished parts. Two historical seeds reaching one point are kept in ecc_public.historical_conflicts; any row there is a collision in the original campaign and needs the solver.
  4. backmatch runs after the last load. Batches indexed before their point was imported never joined against it; it writes the campaign leads that index_one would have written, and the resolver picks them up as usual. It is idempotent. Run it again after any later load.
  5. reconcile (optional) compares per-worker counts with the original RDS view through a read-only SOURCE_DSN. Workers short of the source there need a look; workers ahead of it are the view lagging S3.

First run, 2026-10-17, from historical-import/20261017/: 40,309 objects exported (the 68 <sha256>-<start>-<end>.bin runner deltas included), one witness-format object refused, 189,871,706 DP34 records dropped as above_dp32_weight. 384,765,103 records loaded in two admin-task runs, 338,034,791 distinct points inserted, 0 historical conflicts. Backmatch: 0 matches, as no public ECC2K-130 points had been indexed yet. The original fleet was still writing, so later objects need another export, load and backmatch. Export to the same historical-import/20261017/ prefix: it skips sources that already have a sidecar there, while a new prefix exports everything again.

The status page reads the import's totals through ecc_public.historical_import_totals (sql/007_historical_totals.sql), which the database bootstrap creates and grants to ecc_site_web. Run the bootstrap admin task once after merging that migration. Until it runs, the page shows gateway-only counts and logs historical import totals unavailable; order against the web deploy doesn't matter. Each later load raises the figure within a minute, with no deploy.

Size the database before loading: every historical point is one distinguished_points row of about 90 bytes with its primary key index.

1. Deploy the foundation and private data stack

Run from a clean, committed checkout. Set up a fresh named AWS CLI profile for the new account. Check that STS reports the expected account:

aws --profile NEW_PROFILE sts get-caller-identity --query Account --output text

The first deploy creates the foundation, VPC, private database, archive, and admin ECR repository. It also creates an empty OAuth secret. The scripts print resource IDs and ARNs, never secret values.

python3 scripts/deploy_data.py --profile NEW_PROFILE --account-id NEW_ACCOUNT_ID
python3 scripts/deploy_data.py --profile NEW_PROFILE --account-id NEW_ACCOUNT_ID --apply

The admin image contains the SQL migrations and database bootstrap. Publish it from the same clean commit, then update the data stack using the immutable digest that the publisher prints:

python3 scripts/publish_admin.py --profile NEW_PROFILE --account-id NEW_ACCOUNT_ID
python3 scripts/deploy_data.py --profile NEW_PROFILE --account-id NEW_ACCOUNT_ID \
  --admin-image-uri ADMIN_IMAGE_DIGEST --apply
python3 scripts/run_admin.py --profile NEW_PROFILE --account-id NEW_ACCOUNT_ID
python3 scripts/run_admin.py --profile NEW_PROFILE --account-id NEW_ACCOUNT_ID --apply
python3 scripts/init_registry.py --profile NEW_PROFILE --account-id NEW_ACCOUNT_ID --apply

The admin task runs in a public subnet with an outbound public IP. Its RDS connection stays inside the dedicated VPC and uses verified TLS. It reads the RDS managed master secret and generated role passwords through its task role, installs the public schema, grants narrow privileges, and verifies both application logins. A nonzero task exit is a failed bootstrap; inspect the /ecc-challenges/admin CloudWatch log group, fix the cause, and rerun the idempotent task. The application services must wait for a successful task.

The registry initializer writes only the new account's ready marker using a conditional S3 write. It refuses a wrong account, bucket, or incompatible existing marker.

2. Configure GitHub login and TLS

Use a public GitHub App for contributor sign-in, with homepage https://ecc-challenges.com and callback https://ecc-challenges.com/auth/callback. The site needs only the authenticated user's numeric ID and login from GET /user; this endpoint requires no GitHub App permissions. Disable the webhook unless another feature needs it, and do not grant repository or organization permissions for sign-in. A user can authorize the app without installing it. The App ID and private key are not used by this sign-in flow.

In the new account's Secrets Manager, update ecc-challenges/github-oauth to a JSON object with client_id and client_secret from that GitHub App. Keep the client secret in Secrets Manager; never paste it into chat or source. The empty initial values make service deployment fail closed. The web flow does not request OAuth scopes because GitHub Apps use their configured permissions.

GitHub documents this sign-in flow and the permission-free GET /user endpoint.

Request an ACM certificate in us-west-2 for ecc-challenges.com and www.ecc-challenges.com. Add the certificate's DNS validation CNAMEs in Squarespace and wait until ACM reports ISSUED. DNS records for the original account's certificate do not establish validation for this new certificate. The release script checks the certificate account, region, status, and both hostnames.

3. Publish contributor and service images, then deploy

Publish the contributor image into the new account's ECR Public registry. The publisher creates the repository if needed, verifies its owner, refuses an existing tag, and prints a pinned digest. ECR Public uses the us-east-1 API endpoint even when the service stack is in us-west-2.

python3 scripts/publish_public_worker.py --profile NEW_PROFILE --account-id NEW_ACCOUNT_ID

Pull the printed digest anonymously from a fresh Docker configuration. Use that digest as NEW_PUBLIC_WORKER_DIGEST below. Build and publish the web and audit images from the same clean commit:

python3 scripts/publish_images.py --profile NEW_PROFILE --account-id NEW_ACCOUNT_ID

Read VpcId, DataBucketName, and DatabaseHost from the ecc-challenges-data CloudFormation outputs. The service deployer checks all three against that stack and checks its generated DB password secrets against the foundation. The first command is a read-only plan. Replace the placeholders with the reported IDs, certificate ARN, and image tag:

python3 scripts/deploy_service.py --profile NEW_PROFILE --account-id NEW_ACCOUNT_ID \
  --certificate-arn NEW_CERT_ARN --public-worker-image NEW_PUBLIC_WORKER_DIGEST \
  --vpc-id NEW_VPC_ID \
  --bucket DATA_BUCKET --db-host DB_HOST --tag git-COMMITSHA
python3 scripts/deploy_service.py --profile NEW_PROFILE --account-id NEW_ACCOUNT_ID \
  --certificate-arn NEW_CERT_ARN --public-worker-image NEW_PUBLIC_WORKER_DIGEST \
  --vpc-id NEW_VPC_ID \
  --bucket DATA_BUCKET --db-host DB_HOST --tag git-COMMITSHA \
  --web-tasks 2 --audit-tasks 2 --index-tasks 1 \
  --reconcile-tasks 1 --resolve-tasks 1 --apply

Add --alert-email ADDRESS to the deploy command to subscribe an operator to audit-age, index-age, and dead-letter alarms. The recipient must confirm the Amazon SNS subscription email before notifications can arrive. The alert topic and alarm actions exist even when no email is configured; an unconfirmed or missing subscription is not an operational alert path. Check the subscription status with aws sns list-subscriptions-by-topic using the service stack's AlertTopicArn output, and verify alarm actions before DNS cutover.

Before routing DNS, exercise the ALB with the intended hostname and TLS SNI:

curl --connect-to ecc-challenges.com:443:ALB_DNS:443 \
  https://ecc-challenges.com/health

Require healthy web targets in both zones; GitHub sign-in and key creation; a real NVIDIA contributor container run; first-batch exact replay; indexing of new public candidates; invalid-seed quarantine; and an outbox/SQS restart drill. Verify the contributor image can be pulled anonymously. The dashboard uses the same pinned public digest that the service deployer verified belongs to the new account.

The service stack outputs two Global Accelerator IPv4 addresses and its DNS name. Set both apex A records in Squarespace, use the accelerator DNS name for the www CNAME, and remove conflicting Squarespace defaults. Verify /health, login, and the dashboard through ordinary DNS from outside AWS. The addresses stay stable across ALB changes.

4. Watch and respond

  • Watch ALB 5xx, ECS target health, WAF blocks, S3 errors, RDS CPU/IOPS and connections, queue age/dead-letter counts, and pressure-shard totals.
  • The oldest-audit-message alarm and all three dead-letter queues make a growing ingest backlog visible. Measure producer arrival against audit and index drain before raising admission limits.
  • Treat unverified audits and collision leads as unresolved. Preserve the write-once input and receipt, then retry after the verifier or solver is repaired. A timeout is not a negative mathematical finding.
  • If arrivals exceed sustained drain, lower contributor quotas or suspend admission after preserving queued work. Keep S3 objects, cursor rows, dead-letter messages, and candidate quarantine evidence.

Until the historical import above has run and its backmatch has finished, describe collision coverage as new-public-to-new-public only. While the original fleet is still writing, catch up by rerunning export, load and backmatch: export skips source keys it has already copied and picks up new ones.

All-curve release builds and canary gate

infra/build.yaml provisions one bounded Linux CodeBuild release builder. It clones an explicit public commit, verifies HEAD, builds the four images, runs the native self-test, and writes pinned digests to release-builds/<commit>/manifest.json in the isolated bucket. The build role has image-push and release-manifest permissions, with no database-secret access. No contributor credential enters that build context.

Deploy migration 003 and worker/web images before enabling v2. A rollout can set MulticurveCanaryKey to the ID portion of the designated key while MulticurveEnabled=false. Only that authenticated key can use v2; public catalog availability stays unchanged. The worker queue still processes its batches. After combined-container, contributor and capacity gates, enable v2 and clear the canary parameter. Keep existing v1 workers on their bound namespace.

Retiring a generic contributor run

An ordinary container stop preserves its run for resumption. To switch a worker permanently to another challenge, stop it gracefully and then launch the same pinned image, key, campaign and state volume with ECC_PROTOCOL=2 and ECC_ACTION=close. This authenticates ownership and retires the run without removing its checkpoints, uploaded points or verification work. The command refuses a local pending outbox; resume normal work to flush it first. An unfinished server upload intent must commit or expire before closure. Closed runs remain readable and their admitted batches continue processing. Use a new state volume for a new run. Closing releases an active slot; it does not reset the account's lifetime anti-abuse limit.

V2 admission and verifier scaling

--max-pending-batches is an explicit per-protocol deployment bound (initially 512), sharded across sixteen pressure rows. At the maximum 1 MiB batch size this bounds v2 pending raw payload near 512 MiB; account and daily-byte quotas apply as well. Choose the bound from measured drain time. Contributors keep their outbox and pause on retryable refusal.

The audit pool performs all v2 relation checks and DynamoDB insertion. The separate legacy index pool does not add v2 processing capacity. Audit scale-out uses visible queue depth and CPU utilization, up to 32 tasks. Automatic audit scale-in is disabled during the initial rollout to avoid interrupting long, in-flight verification batches. Review pending work and retained leases before an operator reduces the pool. This can leave extra tasks running after a burst; monitor cost and tune after the sustained capacity gate. The existing scripts/capacity.py models the legacy sampled verifier and cannot establish v2 throughput. A production DP/s claim requires measurements of every distinct witness under the deployed curve mix and fleet size.

Switching the point index to compact S3 parts

The compact index (see docs/multicurve-storage.md, "Compact point index") replaces DynamoDB items with sorted 16-byte entries in S3.

  1. Update the data stack so the bucket gets the lifecycle rule for superseded parts (scripts/deploy_data.py).
  2. Run the database bootstrap so 005_compact_point_index.sql and its grant apply.
  3. Deploy the service with --point-index-mode compact and keep --reconcile-tasks 1. In compact mode the reconcile task grows to 1 vCPU and 4 GB, and merges every --point-index-merge-seconds (default 3600).
  4. Watch the reconcile log for point-index-merge lines. Each one names the generation, the entry count and any collision_leads.

Batches indexed into DynamoDB earlier stay there, so switch before public contribution starts. If the index is ever in doubt, call Merger.rebuild(namespace_id) from an administration task: the next merges rebuild it from the raw batches.

Public image mirrors

ECR Public anonymous consumers have a fixed monthly data allowance. Shared cloud provider importers can exhaust that allowance before starting a container. infra/registry.yaml supplies a public-image authentication role with no push, private-image, bucket, database or application-secret permissions. Its GitHub OIDC trust binds the repository's verified immutable IDs and the release refs.

The existing contributor-image workflow accepts an optional source_image dispatch input. It copies the exact ECR image to ghcr.io/aburan28/ecc-challenges-worker with digest preservation and checks an anonymous pull. First-time GHCR package publication can require the package owner to make it public in GitHub's package settings. Do not advertise the mirror until the anonymous check passes. The deployment helper requires the mirror's manifest bytes to match an image digest in the isolated AWS account.

Internal Modal checks can optionally use a mode-0600 ECC_REGISTRY_AUTH_FILE containing a temporary pull-only token. Sending that token to a third-party importer requires explicit authorization; an automatic approval rejection does not authorize another transport. No AWS access keys belong in a contributor container. The public release must work with an anonymous provider pull.

problems/dp32-verifier-and-ingest-capaci.title: DP32 verifier and ingestion capacity
problems/dp32-verifier-and-ingest-capaci.html:
DP32 verifier and ingestion capacity

Status: open. Scope: the ecc-challenges.com public ECC2K-130 admission gateway at DP weight 32, using the pinned sigma walk, 1 MiB batches, a 1/128 post-seal later-batch audit selection, and the dedicated private rho_dp instance.

Specific obstruction

The exact host replay binary is built and wired to a separate SQS audit pool, but its DP32 replay seconds per selected seed and the sustained audit/index drain rate on release infrastructure have not yet been measured. The CPU walk can require hundreds of millions of steps per report. Without the measured service time and a production-shaped arrival/drain test, the configured 32 audit and eight index task ceilings cannot justify opening to an unbounded global fleet. A growing queue would eventually trigger admission backpressure and local worker spooling; the service would remain durable but would not keep up with the offered load.

This is a resource and validation gap, not a proof that the design cannot scale. The original campaign already has distinguished points in its own RDS instance, but their count does not measure this new verifier or public-gateway throughput. Historical matching remains unavailable until the separate import and backmatch; the public candidate index can match new points to new points. The reserved public run range has 15,535 IDs, which also bounds the number of distinct public run identities without a registry audit or new format. The original campaign's RDS ingress is a separate security exposure outside the public platform and does not establish a throughput result.

What would clear it

  1. Capture a frozen DP32 seed/record pair from the same sigma campaign and exact source/image digests. Replay it independently on the release audit task size; record elapsed seconds, iterations, CPU, memory, exit status, and record byte equality. Repeat across enough distinct trails to report p50 and p95, including a timeout/invalid-seed control.
  2. Run a bounded load with distinct reserved run IDs and sealed batches at 2× the planned contributor arrival rate. Measure S3 ACKs, audit and index queue age, RDS writes/locks/CPU/IOPS, collision outbox, dead-letter counts, ECS scaling, and cost over the same interval. Stop arrivals and show that both queues drain to baseline, with every acknowledged object accounted for.
  3. Simulate one SQS send failure and one task restart; show outbox repair, idempotent replay/indexing, and no lost cursor or duplicate accepted key.

A pass establishes capacity only up to the tested fleet and service limits. It does not guarantee that every unsampled point is valid or that a collision will occur by any deadline. A failure to drain leads to a measured lower admission ceiling, more verifier capacity, or a faster exact verifier before raising the public cap. An invalid-seed control that reaches the candidate index without quarantine blocks release until the integrity path is fixed.

Related prior design and obstruction: aburan28/cryptanalysis, ecc2k130/runner/public/ADMISSION-AND-SCALE.md and problems/ecc2k130-public-gateway-activation.md. The exact service code and current tests are in this repository's src/, verifier/, sql/, and tests/ paths.

problems/multi-campaign-worker-and-verif.title: Certicom multi-campaign worker and verifier
problems/multi-campaign-worker-and-verif.html:
Certicom multi-campaign worker and verifier

Status: open. Scope: admitting distinguished points for the 23 published Certicom exercises and challenges other than ECC2K-130 through the ecc-challenges.com public gateway.

Binary arithmetic throughput obstruction, 2026-10-19

The nine binary campaigns have integrated worker code and finite correctness controls, but the fastest shared arithmetic for sustained Pollard rho work is not established. A bounded-word, branchless binary_xtime candidate was correct on the pinned controls yet slower than the current full-width implementation on a matched NVIDIA L4 panel. All 18 long-panel candidate invocations took longer relative to their bracketing baselines; the pooled candidate/baseline full-process median was 1.208. The ten comparisons whose baseline bracket drift stayed within 1.05 had ratios 1.122–1.360. The candidate was removed from the release diff. See the insight report and raw receipts.

This observation establishes a regression for that candidate on those L4 workloads. It does not identify the cause or prove the present arithmetic optimal. Kernel instruction and register costs, sustained useful-step rate, collection/verification costs, and other hardware remain unmeasured. A specific next test is to retain the same nine pinned job/input pairs, capture kernel-only time and compiler register/instruction output for both headers, then measure a proposed replacement in baseline–candidate–baseline order on the same GPU. Require exact output, distinguished-point and step equality; retain failed runs and raw measurements. A candidate that is faster under stable brackets would justify independent replication and full pipeline accounting. A slower or inconsistent candidate returns to codegen diagnosis. Only a verified complete pipeline comparison can establish a campaign-level improvement; until then this performance requirement remains open.

Current release boundary, 2026-10-16

All 24 published instances now have implemented CPU/CUDA workers and the v2 archive/verifier/index path. The selected published image passed 168 checks on a real L4 as UID/GID10001. All 24 production-predicate CPU contribution checks also passed against the deployed gateway: upload, index, checkpoint resume, and explicit run closure. Exact image/source/S3-version bindings and failed attempts are retained in release evidence.

The remaining obstruction is release validation: a real GPU contribution with a persistent volume, current-head required CI, and a sustained fresh-point capacity envelope. Anonymous GHCR import and all 168 L4 checks passed, and the bounded account-backlog/refusal/restart/drain check passed. The AWS account currently has 30 Fargate vCPUs; request 6b9319d443fe49b882919fe6ebcfeef4QPzCozkp asks for 256. Until effective, the configured 32-auditor ceiling is not available in full.

V2 stays restricted to the designated canary key while these gates are checked. Completion probability remains unavailable because coefficient validity does not verify the claimed number of trail operations. The historical database import ran on 2026-10-17; see docs/operations.md, "Historical point import".

Modal checkpoint access obstruction

After the release PR merged, a CPU-only probe of the selected public image on Modal failed to create /data/probe.tmp as UID/GID10001 after a successful root bootstrap chown('/data', 10001, 10001). No contributor key was supplied. The failure log and receipt are preserved as the first volume-readiness attempt. The local harness reported IndexError while parsing empty stdout; the remote stderr identifies PermissionError13 as the actual checkpoint-write failure.

Modal documents that it ignores Docker USER. Its public Volume documentation does not specify whether mount ownership changes permit another UID to access the filesystem. A mount-level UID restriction is a suspected explanation, not an established diagnosis. This blocks the Modal launcher's persistence guarantee and the real GPU contributor canary; it does not invalidate the completed GPU arithmetic or Fargate contribution checks.

The next bounded diagnostic creates a private child directory as root, records ownership and modes before/after changes, and attempts atomic writes as10001. Acceptance requires two fresh CPU sandboxes to read and advance the same mode0600 checkpoint as UID/GID10001, plus an external committed-volume hash match. An access failure requires a different verified persistence mechanism; repeating chmod/chown without changed evidence is insufficient. A passing probe permits a launcher repair and the separately authorized GPU canary. Sustained fresh-point capacity remains a separate outstanding gate.

The final shared-bootstrap attempt5 met this filesystem acceptance criterion: two fresh CPU sandboxes advanced the same mode0600 file as UID/GID10001, both external committed-volume hashes matched, and the original mount-root file migrated successfully. Its frozen setup SHA is 9211407a376609a5789aa62b2d2dd5ca1d41730d41ad0dd52e92fb8b55f3704a. The provider /data entry was observed to be a symlink. Resolving that trusted entry and creating a private owned child corrected access; persisted child symlinks remain rejected. The first failed production-helper attempt rejected the provider mount symlink itself; it is preserved alongside the earlier failure and successful diagnostic controls in volume-readiness evidence.

This closes the checkpoint-permission obstruction for the tested Modal image and shared bootstrap. The real GPU contribution still requires the separately requested authorization to transmit the contributor key through a runtime Modal Secret. No contributor key was sent during these filesystem controls.

Consumer-stop and queue-baseline check

The first bounded pressure attempt rejected a valid regionless S3 hostname in the harness; its held reservation was completed and indexed normally. The second attempt observed ECS runningCount 0 while the old tasks were STOPPING. Their processes still consumed records, so the intended 32-batch backlog never formed. All 33 acknowledged records subsequently indexed through normal commit replay, with no lease mutation; that recovery receipt is retained separately.

The next preflight refused a nonzero SQS in-flight count. A read-only SQL task then measured 59 indexed v2 batches, zero pending v1/v2 batches or bytes, and zero active processing leases, while SQS retained two invisible deliveries. This is a delivery-versus-work accounting distinction. The raw SQS count alone cannot establish a pending application backlog. No message was purged or deleted to make the check pass.

The corrected bounded check must wait for the exact old task ARNs to become STOPPED. Any nonzero in-flight baseline requires a fresh, source-bound read-only SQL receipt with zero unfinished work/pressure and matching queue counts.
